lessons.title: Catch a type mismatch
lessons.summary: Keep remaining numeric while subtracting three seats.
explanation: TypeScript checks descriptions of values before JavaScript runs. In let seats: number = 6, the colon introduces a written type annotation: seats must hold a number. The annotation is not a conversion. Writing a quoted "6" would still supply text, so the checker rejects that assignment.

If you change seats = 8 to seats = "8", the checker reports that string is not assignable to number. Fix the value or reconsider the intended contract; do not assume the compiler will parse text into a number. A type error and a runtime exception are different events: here the app stops before running the program.

Create remaining as a number initialized to 12, subtract 3, and keep the result in remaining. In the project, the value must be 9 and must still have the number type. An explicit annotation or correct inference is acceptable.
steps: Read the example and its input/output contract.
Complete the starter without turning off compiler diagnostics.
Run the compiler and behavior checks, then explain a changed case.
lessons.starter:
let remaining: number = 12;
// TODO: subtract 3 and store the result
lessons.solution:
let remaining: number = 12;
remaining = remaining - 3;

quiz.question: The example changes to let spare = 2; spare = "2";. What happens before it runs?
choices: The checker rejects the later text assignment because spare was inferred as number.
Inference disables checking after the first assignment.
It converts the text to 2 automatically.
quiz.explanation: The initial numeric value establishes a number type for this mutable variable. Text is a different type, even when its characters look numeric.

hints: Compare the public input/output types and trace the visible call before editing.

typeAssertions.code: type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false; type Assert<T extends true> = T; type Safe=Assert<IsAny<typeof remaining> extends false?true:false>;const n:number=remaining;

lessons.title: Keep array elements one kind
lessons.summary: Append one number to a typed checkpoint list.
explanation: number[] describes an array whose elements are numbers. The brackets here belong to a type description; [3, 6] is the separate runtime array value. A number[] can be empty. It does not promise a fixed length or validate unrelated data from a file.

scores.push("9") is rejected: the array expects number elements, not numeric-looking text. const prevents replacing the scores binding, but it does not freeze the array; the successful push still mutates its contents.

Make checkpoints a number array [2, 5], then append 8. Keep all three values in order. The compiler check also tries an invalid text append, so a broadly untyped array is not equivalent to the requested number array.
steps: Read the example and its input/output contract.
Complete the starter without turning off compiler diagnostics.
Run the compiler and behavior checks, then explain a changed case.
lessons.starter:
const checkpoints: number[] = [2, 5];
// TODO: append 8
lessons.solution:
const checkpoints: number[] = [2, 5];
checkpoints.push(8);

quiz.question: After the worked code, scores.push("12") is added. What does the checker report?
choices: The text argument does not match the number element type.
An array created with const cannot be changed at all.
The checker silently changes the string into a number.
quiz.explanation: The binding is constant, but its array is mutable. The actual problem is the string element, not const or the number of items.

lessons.title: Type a function boundary
lessons.summary: Return twice a numeric points value.
explanation: In function addBonus(points: number): number, the first annotation describes the input parameter points. The annotation after the closing parenthesis describes the return value. The function body must return a compatible value, and each checked call must supply a compatible argument.

addBonus("7") is rejected at the call because it supplies text. Replacing return points + 4 with return "bonus" is rejected in the body because the promised result is numeric. The two checks protect different sides of the same boundary; neither performs runtime input conversion.

Implement doublePoints(points: number): number so it returns twice its input. The task includes zero and negative numbers. Keep the function numeric; producing a string that happens to look correct is not the same contract.
steps: Read the example and its input/output contract.
Complete the starter without turning off compiler diagnostics.
Run the compiler and behavior checks, then explain a changed case.

quiz.question: The call stays addBonus(7), but the body now returns "11". Which boundary fails?
choices: The input is wrong because 7 is a number.
No boundary fails because the displayed characters would look similar.
The body returns text even though the return type promises a number.
quiz.explanation: A numeric input does not make a text return value numeric. The return annotation checks the result separately.

lessons.title: Narrow before using a value
lessons.summary: Use a type check to choose arithmetic or preserved text.
explanation: string | number allows either kind at a function boundary. Before an operation that needs one particular kind, check which kind you actually have. Narrowing is the checker using a runtime condition to learn a more specific type in that branch.

The input "04" does not become 4 just because its characters are digits. typeof distinguishes its actual runtime kind. No parsing is performed here. A condition about the value also helps the compiler allow only operations appropriate to that path.

Implement describeCount(value: string | number): string. For numbers return "Next " followed by value + 1; for text return "Label " followed by the unchanged text. Both supported input kinds must be accepted.

lessons.title: Preserve literal information
lessons.summary: Keep a coordinate literal precise and readonly.
explanation: as const asks the checker to retain literal values and readonly properties for this literal expression. For [2, 4], it produces a readonly two-position tuple rather than a general mutable number array. A tuple describes fixed positions with separately known types; here those positions retain the literal types 2 and 4. For {kind:"home"}, kind keeps the literal type "home" and is readonly through this typed value.

The checker rejects position[0] = 9 through this readonly tuple. Ordinary const only protects the binding; as const additionally changes the inferred type of the literal. A precise explicitly written readonly type can express an equivalent contract.
Create originPoint as a readonly two-position tuple with values 0 and 0, retaining each literal type 0. An as const assertion or an equivalent explicit readonly tuple type is accepted.
steps: Read the example and its input/output contract.
Complete the starter without turning off compiler diagnostics.
Run the compiler and behavior checks, then explain a changed case.

lessons.solution: const originPoint = [0, 0] as const;

It rejects the write because that tuple position is readonly, even when the value is unchanged.
quiz.explanation: Readonly forbids assignment through that typed reference. The restriction is about writing, not whether the new value would be different.

lessons.title: Extend an object description
lessons.summary: Reuse a name field in a scored record.
explanation: An interface describes an object shape. TimedItem extends NamedItem means a TimedItem must have NamedItem’s title property as well as its own minutes property. extends here combines checked descriptions; it does not copy runtime data or create a class inheritance relationship.

lessons.title: Read a declaration beside real JavaScript
lessons.summary: Explain why a declaration can type-check while a missing JavaScript implementation still fails at runtime.
explanation: A .d.ts file describes names and types for the compiler; it supplies no executable implementation. Here labels.d.ts declares a function named label accepting a string and returning a string. The matching labels.js actually creates that function. A declaration can be wrong, so type-checking does not verify an arbitrary JavaScript implementation.

This is a local-only workflow, not the app runner. Use an isolated folder with Node and an already installed TypeScript 5.9.3 compiler (verify tsc --version). package.json marks CommonJS for Node; exports.label publishes the JavaScript function on that module’s exports object. main.ts imports the declaration by the same module name, and generated CommonJS JavaScript loads the real labels.js.

File package.json
```json
{"type":"commonjs"}
```

File labels.js
```javascript
exports.label = function(text) { return "Label: " + text; };
```

File labels.d.ts
```typescript
export declare function label(text: string): string;
```

File main.ts
```typescript
import { label } from "./labels";
console.log(label("Stars"));
```

From that folder run:
```sh
tsc --strict --target ES2015 --module commonjs --noEmitOnError main.ts
node main.js
```
The compiler emits main.js beside main.ts. It uses the declaration for checking; Node uses labels.js for execution. label("Stars") returns Label: Stars, which console.log displays. --noEmitOnError prevents new output when compilation reports an error; it does not delete stale files.

Optional local practice: rename labels.js temporarily while retaining labels.d.ts and rebuild. Compilation can still succeed, but running main.js fails to load the implementation. Restore the file afterward. No browser-import support is implied.

quiz.question: Remove only labels.js, leaving the declaration and importing source. What can happen?
choices: Compilation succeeds, but Node fails to load the implementation.
The declaration automatically generates the function body.
The compiler must execute the implementation before accepting the import.
quiz.explanation: The .d.ts supplies a static contract, not executable code. Runtime module loading still needs the real JavaScript.

lessons.title: Separate emitted syntax from available APIs
lessons.summary: Compare two local outputs and explain why compiler API declarations do not install runtime features.
explanation: target chooses the JavaScript syntax level to emit; lib supplies declarations for APIs the compiler may assume; module chooses module handling/output; strict enables a group of stricter checks. None installs runtime APIs. Raising lib alone does not add missing methods to an old browser.

Use Node and TypeScript 5.9.3 in an isolated local folder. This app does not expose these settings as learner controls. The two configurations below keep lib, module and strict identical and change target. ES5 lowers the arrow to a function; ES2015 can retain the arrow. CommonJS handles the exported doubled binding in both. DOM is included here for console declarations, not because Node becomes a browser.

Run:
```sh
tsc -p tsconfig.es5.json
tsc -p tsconfig.es2015.json
node out-es5/main.js
node out-es2015/main.js
```
-p selects a configuration; files names the source and outDir separates outputs. map calls its callback once for each array element and returns a new array of doubled numbers. join(",") returns a comma-separated string. Both programs display 4,10 on the tested Node host; inspect the two main.js files to see their different arrow syntax. This is not evidence that every ES5 environment provides every API.

Optional local practice: change only lib to ["ES2015"]. The program still names console, but its declaration is missing from these chosen libraries, so compilation fails. This does not prove Node lacks a console. Restore the configuration before running; old output files may remain after failed builds.

quiz.question: What does adding an API declaration through lib guarantee?
choices: The target setting becomes irrelevant to generated syntax.
The browser receives a polyfill automatically.
Only that the compiler can know its declared shape, not that the runtime implements it.
quiz.explanation: lib provides compile-time declarations. Runtime support, emitted syntax and module execution are separate concerns.
